To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the accounting curriculum in the UK is not fit-for-purpose.

(1) accounting students have the knowledge of accounting and are able to perform the accounting processes; (2) the accounting knowledge and processes are taught in a manner that is not conducive to students' learning and (3) accounting education is a "one-size-fits-all" approach that is not responsive to students' needs and learning styles.

(i) accounting education is not a major determinant of career success; (ii) the relationship between accounting education and career success is not linear; and (iii) accounting education is more important for some careers than for others.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an understanding of the role of accounting education and the nature of accounting education in the UK.

the nature and extent of the changes that have taken place in the accounting curriculum over the last two or three decades and the extent to which they have been driven by the perceived need to produce graduates who are more employable.

the extent to which accounting students are prepared for the workplace by their education and the extent to which their education has been successful in developing the knowledge and skills required to be an effective professional accountant.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the accounting curriculum was too academic and too theoretical and did not prepare students for the practicalities of the workplace.
the accounting education process in many universities was failing to prepare students for the workplace.
the criticisms were justified and that accounting educators were slow to respond.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have been responding to the criticisms by developing and implementing a variety of initiatives.

accounting education has been re-engineered to respond to the criticisms and the result has been the introduction of a new breed of accounting graduates, who, in the UK at least, have been described as "accountants in the making" rather than "accountants in being".
the accounting education community has responded to these criticisms in two ways.
The main takeaway from our work is that
accounting education is a process of learning and not just the acquisition of knowledge.
there is an important role for accounting educators and employers in developing a shared understanding of the skills, attributes, and knowledge required of accounting graduates.
the criticisms are still relevant today.
